- After 5.7 weeks, net progress is −1 rung on the left and 0 on the right; 7 of 12 arm-exposures were not PASS.
- A left-arm memo blames a HOLD on the awkward rung-1 grip, not on strength.
- Exposure is about 1.05 per week, against the spec's about 1.5.
- The '≥2 weeks on a new rung' guideline has no compliant way to be followed when the engine promotes.
evidence: Internal record, left arm: 9/07 r2 FAIL, 9/12 r2 FAIL → r1, 9/21 HOLD (memo: awkward rung-1 grip on the left, may have had strength left), 9/24 HOLD, 10/04 PASS, 10/14 PASS.
Internal record, right arm: 9/07 and 9/12 FAIL → r1; 9/21, 9/24 and 10/04 PASS → r2; 10/14 HOLD.
Spec §22.4.11 (ordinal scale) and §19.5.1(c) (2-week dwell, not enforced).

leverage.fit, Hybrid Calisthenics and Brookshire (coaching): finger or hand assistance is hard to measure; positions past the elbow are awkward. https://www.hybridcalisthenics.com/advanced-onehand-pullups
Bohm et al. 2015: tendon adaptation was studied only in interventions of 8 weeks or longer, so 2 weeks is untested as an adaptation window. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-015-0009-9
coaching.reasoning: The record facts are direct. That assist force and grip ergonomics, not strength, drive part of the variance is an inference supported by the memo and by coaching sources. Five exposures per arm cannot separate insufficient stimulus from insufficient recovery. At about 1 exposure per week, the 2-week dwell will usually happen by accident anyway.
coaching.recommendation: Operational. Fix and note the assisting-hand contact (same grip type and the same 'support only as needed' cue on both arms) for the rest of the plan, so exposures stay comparable. Propose a rung-definition refinement under §26 only if the v1.4 oscillation trigger in §23 (3 promote/demote cycles on one arm) fires.

coaching.claim: Session order puts the priority lift first every session: squat first, and focus 3×3 before volume work. This matches the exercise-order evidence. The cost is that OAP, now the athlete's #1 upper-body goal and a skill/lock-off task, sits third, after SQ and BP 3×3. There, fatigue may blunt both performance and skill learning.
evidence: Nunes JP et al. 2021: multi-joint strength favoured performing the exercise first (ES 0.32); gains are largest for exercises at the start of a session. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32077380/
ACSM 2026: strength is enhanced when the exercise is performed at the beginning of the session. https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897
Lopez-Rivera 2013 (coaching): lock-off training should come at the beginning of the workout, after a warm-up. http://en-eva-lopez.blogspot.com/2013/05/lock-off-training-for-climbers-v-goal.html
Branscheidt et al. 2019: practising while fatigued impaired motor-skill learning beyond the session (partly central; lab finger task). https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.40578
Internal record: OAP 7/12 arm-exposures not PASS; spec §7.3 order is SQ → BP focus → OAP → OHP.
coaching.reasoning: SQ-first support is direct. The OAP-placement cost is extrapolation from order meta-analyses and a lab skill-learning study, plus coaching opinion. Moving OAP earlier would push BP focus later, with a predictable BP cost under the same order evidence. Five exposures cannot attribute the OAP results to order.
coaching.recommendation: A §26-style single proposal, not a directive. On BP-focus days, move the OAP slot to position 2 (SQ → OAP → BP focus → OHP), keeping squat first. Do this only if the §21.1 review shows no net rung gain. Expected cost: somewhat lower BP-focus performance.

coaching.claim: The undiagnosed suprapatellar (quadriceps-tendon-insertion) pain is the most likely non-program limiter of G1, and the program has no structured pain signal. Twice-weekly heavy, non-failure high-bar squats are a tendon-friendly kind of loading. However, the squat stance has changed at least twice within the program (7/24 wider for knee pain; 10/04 narrower), which also weakens how comparable the exposures are.
evidence: Breda et al. 2021, BJSM, JUMPER RCT: progressive tendon loading beat eccentric training (VISA-P +28 vs +18); progression was gated on pain ≤3/10 on a standard provocation test. https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/55/9/501
Agergaard et al. 2021: heavy (90%) and moderate (55%) slow resistance gave similar long-term outcomes in patellar tendinopathy. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0363546520988741
Bohm et al. 2015: tendon stiffness adapts to high-intensity (>70%) loading. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-015-0009-9
Crossley et al. 2016: patellofemoral pain overlaps in presentation; pain during a squat is the best available test. https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/50/14/839
King et al. 2019: few studies focus on quadriceps tendinopathy. https://atm.amegroups.org/article/view/23948
Rio et al. 2015 (n=6): isometric pain relief; small, short follow-up. https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/49/19/1277
Internal record memos 7/24 and 10/04; brief: pain on stairs and sit-to-stand, managed outside the program.
coaching.reasoning: Evidence for quadriceps tendinopathy is sparse and mostly extrapolated from patellar tendinopathy. Without a diagnosis, patellofemoral pain is also plausible, and depth and load guidance differ between them. That REF5's load profile suits tendon adaptation is an extrapolation. Keeping pain outside the judgment system follows the user's own design and does not relax any criterion.
coaching.recommendation: Operational, outside the protocol. The morning after each SQ session, rate knee pain 0–10 on one fixed provocation test (for example, a bodyweight single-leg squat to the same depth) and log it. A clinical assessment to separate patellofemoral pain from quadriceps tendinopathy is also advised.

coaching.claim:
The fixed caps C7 and C8 are applied through REF baselines that understate this athlete's DL and OHP, so both lifts sit at roughly maintenance intensity:
- DL: 75 kg is about 64–67% of e1RM, and a DL window of 4 PASS exposures was discarded because the squat increase came 2 days later.
- OHP: 32.5 kg is about 56–59% of e1RM. It has been frozen since 8/24 through 8 straight PASS, and cannot move until BP focus reaches 90. A +2.5 kg OHP step is 7.7% of the load, vs about 2.9% for SQ.
This is a cost of the user's fixed constraints combined with the REF baselines.
evidence: Internal record: DL REF baseline 100 at 72.5 kg vs DL e1RM ≈112–117. Historical OHP/BP e1RM ratio ≈0.58 vs cap 0.398 × BP focus. 8/11 DL window MAINTAIN by cap; OHP MAINTAIN by cap in Plan B.
Spiering et al. 2021: strength is maintained with low dose if intensity is kept (younger general adults, not athletes). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33629972/
Androulakis-Korakakis et al. 2020: the minimal effective dose for trained men used sets to failure 2–3 times a week; deadlift data are lacking. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31797219/
Räntilä & Ahtiainen 2026: extra volume did not help, and the deadlift favoured lower volume. https://journal.hep.com.cn/josisae/EN/10.1007/s42978-026-00387-7
Plotkin et al. 2022: rep progression at fixed load is a viable overload route in trained adults. https://peerj.com/articles/14142/
Zourdos (SBS, coaching): on a stall, repeat the load or add a rep or set. https://www.strongerbyscience.com/weekly-load-progression/
coaching.reasoning: The intensities are record and engine facts. That this dose maintains rather than builds DL and OHP is an extrapolation, because minimum-dose studies used sets to failure. The low priority is the user's choice (C6–C8), so this describes a cost. Plotkin used lower-body sets to failure at 8–12RM, so applying it to non-failure OHP is indirect.
coaching.recommendation: A §26-style single proposal, low priority. While OHP is frozen by the cap, progress OHP reps at a fixed load (2×6 → 2×8) under the existing all-PASS rule, keeping the load within C8. DL and OHP judgment criteria are unchanged.

coaching.claim: G1 (175 kg high-bar at about 70 kg, 2.5×BW) is a rare, upper-tier outcome. It needs about +70% on an estimated ~103 kg 1RM. At a sustained 5–10% per year that takes roughly 5.6–11 years, and real gains usually slow over time. REF5 cannot confirm attainment, because REF is not a 1RM. The program is a reasonable vehicle for the goal, but it is not a predictor of reaching it.
evidence: Gonzalez et al. 2025, Appl Sci: low-bar 1RM about 7% higher than high-bar in men. https://doi.org/10.3390/app15063143 ; Nuckols (coaching): typically 5–10%. https://www.strongerbyscience.com/its-time-to-end-this-nonsense-high-bar-vs-low-bar-squatting/

Latella et al. 2019: raw 74 kg class squat means were 172.7 kg (local) vs 200.2 kg (international). https://acuresearchbank.acu.edu.au/download/f50fbd80af80bb0182c6d2df3de9874197aaf9db5354cacaff4089cf71d01cde/280151/Latella_2019_Differences_in_Strength_Performance_Between_Novice.pdf
van den Hoek et al. 2024: drug-tested male 90th percentile squat about 2.83×BW in young adults. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2024.07.005
StrengthLog: 95th percentile at 70 kg is 157 kg. https://www.strengthlog.com/squat-strength-standards-kg/
Latella et al. 2024: about 7.5–12.5% in year 1, up to about 20% after 10 years in powerlifters. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01962-6
Nuckols 2018 (coaching analysis): median monthly gain fell from 0.78% to 0.26% over about 770 days. https://www.strongerbyscience.com/?p=46506
Spec §20: REF or REF ÷ bodyweight cannot confirm a real 175 kg.
coaching.reasoning: Rarity: 175 kg high-bar is about 184–193 kg low-bar-equivalent (2.6–2.75× at 70 kg), above the local 74 kg competitor mean and below the drug-tested 90th percentile. That is reasonably well anchored, with medium confidence. The timeline is constant-rate arithmetic against data from selected competitors and is low confidence. The athlete's history (1-year plateau under suboptimal programs) could allow faster early gains, while the deficit and the knee could slow them.
coaching.recommendation: Doc-only. State G1 as a multi-year direction with an interim measurable KPI: the trend of control REF ÷ 7-day measured bodyweight. Keep the spec's statement that REF cannot prove 175 kg.

coaching.claim: G6 (first one-arm chin-up) is plausible but limited by pulling strength relative to bodyweight, not by how fast the ladder can promote. Practitioner heuristics put the threshold around a two-arm chin-up with +60–67% of bodyweight added. The athlete's tested total was 110 kg at 75 kg, about +47% of bodyweight. The planned cut to 70 kg would narrow the relative gap by roughly 7–8 kg-equivalent. On the other side, v1.4 reduced PULL sets, and the logged bodyweight is a default, so the real gap is uncertain.
evidence: Legendary Strength 2018, quoting Willoughby (heuristic): one one-arm chin ≈ a two-arm chin with +2/3 bodyweight. https://legendarystrength.com/chinups-two-arm-one-arm-weighted/
J Aust Strength Cond 2019 9-step model (practitioner): 3RM chin-up at +60% bodyweight before one-arm negatives and partials. https://lida.sport-iat.de/ta/Record/4058980?lng=en
DeMarco (coaching anecdote): start specific work at about +2/3 bodyweight; about 3 years to the first one-arm chin. https://divergentstrengthacademy.com/blog/one-arm-chinups
Lopez-Rivera 2013: lock-off and elbow adaptation takes 'years'. http://en-eva-lopez.blogspot.com/2013/05/lock-off-training-for-climbers-v-goal.html
Internal: ladder minimum ≥15 PASS exposures per arm (≥10–14 weeks). Spec §22.4.9: PULL weekly sets drop from about 8 to about 6. Bodyweight logged as a default.
coaching.reasoning: No peer-reviewed study links weighted pull-up strength to one-arm chin-up achievement or timing. Everything here is coaching heuristics, so confidence is low. The arithmetic: at 75 kg, the Willoughby rule implies a total of about 125 kg (+15 kg vs 110). At 70 kg it is about 117 kg, so the cut alone closes about half the gap if pulling strength holds.
coaching.recommendation: Display only: track PULL focus total ÷ measured bodyweight as the G6 readiness proxy next to the rung state. No protocol change.

evidence: Wendler 2021, Krypteia: main lifts rotate over 2 weeks. https://www.jimwendler.com/blogs/jimwendler-com/krypteia-2-days-week
Lift Vault, nSuns: TM 90%, 9 main sets including AMRAP plus 8 secondary sets per session. https://liftvault.com/programs/powerlifting/n-suns-lifting-spreadsheets/
Liftosaur, Tactical Barbell Operator: wave 63–85% 1RM, ≥80% only in weeks 3 and 6, 'no AMRAP' and 'no built-in auto-regulation'. https://www.liftosaur.com/programs/tactical-barbell-operator
GZCLP (r/Fitness wiki): AMRAPs stop with about 1–2 RIR 'when bar speed slows noticeably'. https://thefitness.wiki/routines/gzclp/
JTS Russian seminar: average intensity about 70%, lifters 'rarely ever miss a rep'. https://www.jtsstrength.com/what-i-learned-at-the-russian-strength-seminar/
Wendler 2024: 'When there is a doubt, there is no doubt'; progress at a plateau takes months. https://www.jimwendler.com/blogs/jimwendler-com/building-strength-and-the-training-max
Fyfe et al. 2022: minimal-dose training may limit negative affective responses that hurt adherence. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-021-01605-8
Internal record: 14 Plan-B sessions over 5.7 weeks; median 47 min from the first squat work set to save; 4 micros, 3 of them automatic.
coaching.reasoning: This is a coaching-level comparison. None of these programs has controlled trials of its own, and several descriptions come from secondary summaries. The match between REF5's design and the athlete's reported failures is a direct reading of the program documents and the athlete's history. That this improves outcomes is a hypothesis the next 2–3 months of data will test (see R5-07).
